faq.q: How does a tree know autumn is coming?
faq.a: Trees sense the nights getting longer and the temperature dropping. These signals switch off chlorophyll making and start the growth of a seal across each leaf stalk.
asks: What tells trees it is autumn?

faq.q: Where do the yellow and orange colours come from?
faq.a: From carotenoids, the same kind of pigment that makes carrots orange. They are in the leaf all summer, helping to catch light, but the strong green of chlorophyll hides them.

faq.q: Why do some leaves turn red?
faq.a: Red comes from anthocyanins, which some trees make fresh in autumn from sugars trapped in the leaf. Scientists think they may act like a sunscreen while the tree pulls nutrients back into its branches.
asks: What makes leaves red in autumn?

faq.q: Why are autumn colours brighter in some years?
faq.a: A run of sunny days and cool but not freezing nights gives the brightest reds, because more sugar is made and trapped in the leaves. An early hard frost or a drought can turn leaves brown and make them fall quickly.
asks: What weather makes the best autumn colours?

faq.q: Why do dead leaves go brown?
faq.a: When the coloured pigments have broken down, brown substances called tannins are left behind. That is why fallen leaves on the ground end up brown.

facts: Carotenoids, the yellow and orange pigments, are present in leaves all summer but hidden by chlorophyll.
Anthocyanins, the red pigments of autumn leaves, are mostly made new in autumn.
Before leaves fall, trees pull back nutrients such as nitrogen from them to reuse in spring.
